title: Interoperability vs. Security: Why not both?
body:
An open internet where people can freely build, share, and remix each other's work is a powerful engine of grassroots innovation we’ve all benefited from. In recent decades, however, corporations have taken control of an increasing share of this work, giving them a greater ability to stifle challengers and limit our choices. When regulators address this by mandating that  tech giants play fair by requiring interoperability, the gatekeepers respond with a tired refrain: Playing fair puts users’ security at risk.  
  Unfortunately for these trillion-dollar companies, this     gotcha     isn’t the end of the conversation. Regulators can ensure that meaningful choice    and    security thrive.  
  Lawmakers have been catching up, recognizing that the best way to rein in big tech is to require these    oligopolies    to open up their platforms to independent developers. As we    explained six years ago   , mandating interoperability helps prevent the misuse of people’s data and enables more privacy-respecting alternatives. Tech giants, in contrast, have been arguing that our data is safer when they have exclusive control.

title: EFF to Brazil’s ANPD: Data Privacy and Free Expression Must Underpin Platform Regulations
body:
The Brazilian National Data Protection Agency (ANPD) plays a pivotal role in the regulation of digital platforms according to new legislation approved in Brazil. Throughout this year, EFF has presented comments, filed submissions, and met with the agency to emphasize crucial guardrails that the enforcement of new regulations should ensure.     
  ANPD is responsible for detailing and applying obligations set in Law n. 15.211/2025, which established rules for the protection of children and adolescents in the digital space. While some provisions establish important privacy safeguards, like prohibiting advertising based on profiling of underage users, the law created mandatory age assurance mechanisms for accessing digital products and services.     
  We have   raised alarms   on the privacy and free expression issues around age-gating the internet.   Age verification technology is often    inaccurate    and    privacy-invasive   .    Examples also show    how it’s prone to enforcement overreach, resulting in sites blocked beyond legal requirements. title: EFF’s State Legislative Agenda to End ALPR Mass Surveillance
body: Police agencies across the U.S. have deployed Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs) to capture images of passing vehicles along with time, date, and GPS coordinates. While the technology itself isn’t new (ALPRs have existed in various forms for  more than 50 years , and in  the U.S. since 1998 ), the surveillance landscape has shifted dramatically. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence and national data sharing have transformed police ALPRs into an interconnected, nationwide tracking network. It is pitched to city councils by law enforcement and private vendors like Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), and Axon as an essential tool for solving violent crime.  In reality, it is an inherently dangerous infrastructure of mass surveillance.  Since  2012 , EFF has worked with others to expose the severe digital rights harms of ALPR systems. For example, we’ve recently documented how these camera networks allow law enforcement to  search for immigrants ,  track peaceful protesters , target  Romani communities , and  track women seeking reproductive healthcare . title: Victory! Court Rules OPM Data Disclosure to DOGE Is Unlawful
body:
In a victory for data privacy,  a federal court in New York definitively ruled  that the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) violated the law when it disclosed millions of federal employee records to DOGE agents. In a summary judgment ruling issued on October 20, 2026, the court found that OPM violated two provisions of the Privacy Act—one restricting disclosure of personal records between agencies and another requiring agencies to protect the security and confidentiality of records. 
 Since the case was filed, many DOGE agents have left the government and OPM has rescinded their database access. However, OPM should still clean up the cybersecurity mess it created. The court will decide the remedy at a later date. 
 "By virtue of the Court’s summary judgment ruling, OPM’s decision to grant DOGE Agents broad access to its systems of recordings containing [personally identifiable information (PII)] has been held unlawful," Judge Denise Cote wrote. 
 "The record also provides no support for a finding that it was the pursuit of a modernization agenda that prompted OPM to grant sweeping and expedited access to a score of DOGE Agents to its systems of records containing PII," she added.

title: Require Police to Get a Warrant to Search ALPR Data
body:
This post was co-written by     Andi Cao    , an EFF legal intern.  
 Automated license plate readers (ALPRs) are mass surveillance. They photograph every passing car and log where and when it was captured, building a searchable record of where nearly everyone drives.   Cities should not buy them  , and cities that already have them should shut them down. 
 Where these systems still operate, courts and state legislatures must reduce their harms by (among other things) requiring police to get a warrant before searching stored ALPR data. A warrant requirement would not make mass surveillance acceptable, but it would require police to justify a search to a judge before accessing records of people’s movements. Without this independent judicial check on police power, officers have been searching this data for improper reasons (many exposed by EFF) that violate our fundamental rights. 
 A warrant requires a judge to find probable cause and specificity—many warrantless police searches of ALPR data lack both. title: EFF Launches Privacy Badger for Safari on macOS
body:
Free Tracker Blocker Used by Millions Will Protect Even More Users' Privacy       SAN FRANCISCO—Privacy Badger, the  award-winning  tracker blocker made by the member-supported digital rights nonprofit  Electronic Frontier Foundation  (EFF), is now available for Safari on macOS.   
 Safari users can  download the free browser extension  today and join the more than 4 million people using Privacy Badger to take a stand against data brokers and online surveillance. Users will need Safari version 26.5 or higher to use it. 
 Ranked as one of the best ad tracker blockers by  The Wirecutter ,  Consumer Reports ,  PC Mag  and more, Privacy Badger is different from other blocking extensions. Created by EFF to stop companies from spying on you online, Privacy Badger  automatically learns  to block hidden trackers on the web, along with additional privacy-protecting features.  
 "Most websites contain invisible tracking code that lets companies collect, share, and profit from your personal data," said Lena Cohen, Staff Technologist at EFF. title: In Memoriam: Barry Steinhardt
body:
Barry Steinhardt, a lifelong privacy champion and an early leader in the battle for digital civil liberties who served as EFF’s president in 1998-99, died last week at age 73.     
  A Connecticut native, Steinhardt led the Vermont and Pennsylvania affiliates of the American Civil Liberties Union before becoming associate director of the national ACLU. There, he helped spearhead the fight to overturn much of the Communications Decency Act, resulting in the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark     Reno v. ACLU     ruling in 1997.     
  When the internet was still young,   Steinhardt   became one of   the first   attorneys to   specialize in the intersection of technology and privacy  .   In early 1998 he took a leave of absence from the ACLU to become EFF’s president, and then returned to the ACLU in 1999.     
  In 2002 he founded the ACLU’s Program on Technology and Liberty. After retiring from the ACLU, he continued on as a senior advisor to London-based  Privacy International .

title: Our Lawsuit Against the Trump Administration’s Social Media Surveillance Moves Forward. Here’s What the Court Said.
body:
No one should have to choose between speaking freely and protecting their immigration status. Yet that’s precisely the choice the Trump administration’s mass surveillance of online speech forces on noncitizens living in the U.S.       
  Last fall, we    sued    on behalf of three major labor unions to stop this surveillance program. And just this month, we won our first major ruling: A federal district court    denied    the government’s motion to dismiss our lawsuit. This means the case can move forward—a win for free speech and a critical step in protecting our First Amendment rights online. We’ve already explained why this is a    big deal    for our clients, so let's take a closer look at the court’s reasoning.      
   Our Lawsuit      
   Since taking power, the Trump administration has used AI and other automated tools to    broadly surveil    the social media and online speech of visa and green card holders, with the goal of identifying and punishing people who express views it opposes. title: We’re Asking the Wisconsin Supreme Court to End Warrantless ALPR Searches
body:
Today, EFF joined the ACLU of Wisconsin in filing a  petition  to the Wisconsin Supreme Court, asking it to rule that the state’s constitution requires a warrant for retrospective searches of ALPR databases used by law enforcement in four cities: Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha, and Green Bay. We represent a religious organization, the Wisconsin Council of Churches, as well as an individual pastor in Green Bay. 
 As the petition explains: 
  Right now, Automated License Plate Readers (“ALPRs”) are recording the movements of vast numbers of Wisconsin drivers as they seek medical care, attend 12-step recovery meetings, attend religious services, participate in protests, attend political meetings, and engage in many other private, sensitive activities. Law enforcement entities throughout Wisconsin collect, store, share, and aggregate this ALPR data. Then they search it, retrospectively tracking the movements of individuals and entire communities in ways that would have been prohibitively costly, if not outright impossible, before the advent of ALPR technology.

title: DHS Inspector General Finds That TSA is Not Properly Safeguarding Passenger Facial Recognition Data
body:
EFF legal intern Gabrielle Ladun was the principal author of this post.      
  The Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General (DHS OIG) has    published a summary of findings    from its audit of the Transportation Security Administration’s (TSA) facial recognition technology. While the detailed findings are classified, the summary states that the OIG’s audit uncovered a “significant weakness” in the technology’s ability to protect the privacy of passenger data. This has massive privacy implications for the millions of passengers who travel and don’t opt out of the TSA’s biometric surveillance technology verification process.   
  TSA uses facial comparison technology for identity verification of airline passengers. A camera takes a photo of passengers to verify that their provided identification matches their live photo. Although TSA states that it is “ committed to protecting traveler privacy ,”   the audit highlights that this has not been the case.

title: As Federal Court Rules ALPRs are Mass Surveillance, EFF Gets Disappointing Ruling
body:
In an extremely disappointing  ruling , a California trial court dismissed   SIREN v. San Jose  , our case challenging the city of San Jose’s warrantless searches of its vast stores of automated license plate reader (ALPR) data. EFF and the ACLU of Northern California represent SIREN and CAIR California, two non-profits that serve San Jose residents, in this case. 
 Make no mistake: We believe this ruling is wrong on the law, and we will appeal. The ruling ignores the importance of landmark rulings from the U.S. Supreme Court regarding the invasiveness of aggregating collected data on an individual over time, including  one issued just months ago . It also severely underestimates the harm that ALPRs cause, in San Jose and around the country.  
 San Jose’s ALPR surveillance system is inescapable. It blankets the city’s streets in nearly five hundred cameras that continuously photograph every car that passes by and retains the collected data for a month or longer. In our briefs, we argued that law enforcement officers who warrantlessly search the resulting ALPR database are violating the California Constitution’s ban on unreasonable searches and its guarantee of privacy. title: Privacy's Defenders Podcast: No Privacy Without Encryption
body:
When we communicate online today – from your personal emails and DMs to secure international commerce – we usually do so with encryption. Encryption converts readable data into unreadable gibberish to protect our privacy and security. This didn’t just happen organically. Three decades ago, the U.S government treated encryption like a weapon, and it took some unlikely heroes to set it free: a grad student, a junior lawyer, and a fledgling digital rights group who sued the federal government.     
  The ruling in     Bernstein v. Department of Justice     held that code is speech and so is protected by the First Amendment – a precedent that underpins the internet as we know it today. This landmark case was led by Cindy Cohn, then a young pro bono lawyer working on behalf of EFF, who went on to become EFF’s legal director and then executive director.     
  Welcome to the second episode of “Privacy’s Defenders,” a podcast about the people – lawyers, journalists, hackers, and others – who’ve fought to secure your digital liberties since before most people even knew what the internet was.

title: Resisting the Menace of Federal Data Consolidation
body:
In the past two years, the federal government has unlawfully  consolidated data  exposing our private information.  
 This consolidation has been chaotic but generally came in three rolling waves: It started with DOGE, moved to agency-to-agency data sharing with ICE, and then attempted data-driven purges of state voter rolls. 
 We all deserve to live in a world where the data we use to pay our taxes, receive benefits, and vote is not combined and weaponized against us. The amalgamation of data leads to mistakes, abuses, and a lack of trust in institutions meant to protect us. Overall, it can chill our participation in society. This is particularly true for groups disfavored by this administration—especially immigrants and protesters. 
 Congress highlighted similar abuses—including the creation of enemies lists and snooping on activists and federal employees—following the McCarthy and Watergate eras. And the increasing use of computers to magnify those harms led Congress to pass a slate of protections like the federal  Privacy Act  of 1974.

title: Organizing in the Town at Oakland Tech Week
body:
EFF was thrilled to join organizers, advocates, and activists in the East Bay for the second annual  Oakland Tech Week  last week. We are grateful to our friends at  MediaJustice  and  Upturn  for inviting us co-present this all-day event,  “Building Beyond Big Tech: Organizing Oakland’s Future” , on Sept. 30.  The event, hosted by the  Kapor Center  in downtown Oakland, offered a unique chance to spend time with people across The Town and the Bay Area working to create a better future for everyone. 
 “We’re at this truly consequential moment,” said EFF executive director Nicole Ozer, in her speech kicking off the day’s events. “We know that in this community’s work—and communities across the country—our ability to  ensure that technology empowers  rather than  oppresses  is fundamental to the future of countries, our livelihoods, and, literally, our lives.” 
 We also participated in a panel on the state of play in California, moderated by MediaJustice executive director Steven Renderos. title: Turkish Crackdown On LGBTQ+ Organizations Threatens Freedom of Expression and Association
body:
EFF strongly condemns    Turkey’s state-led discriminatory, oppressive attacks    on feminist and LGBTQ+ organisations, media platforms, student groups, and rights defenders and activists within the country.   
  Since mid-September, access to the websites and social media accounts of a dozen organizations have been    blocked by court order   , while over 60 members and activists have been detained, their offices and homes    raided   , mobile phones, laptops and other digital devices seized, and judicial proceedings launched against them.   
  These actions threaten the very existence of the LGBTQ+ organizations targeted, limiting their ability to carry out legitimate human rights work, deterring participation and support, and chilling the free speech rights of not just these groups, but any organization that even reports on LGBTQ+ oppression.  
  A little over a week ago, an Istanbul court    shut down the website and social media accounts of T24   , Turkey’s longest running independent digital news organization—which has covered government-backed campaigns against and earlier crackdowns on gay rights groups—alleging it had aired “LGBT propaganda” over the past year.

body:
This post was co-authored by      Sheila B. Lalwani     , a doctorate student and recent      COMPASS Fellow      hosted by EFF.   
  Age verification proposals are    often presented    as a simple tradeoff: sacrifice a little privacy to better safeguard children online. But that framing overlooks a more fundamental question. What happens to people who cannot verify their age at all? This is particularly a problem when users are required to prove their age with identity documents.

title: Site-Blocking Will Not Defend IP, No Matter the Bill’s Name
body:
There has been a raft of site-blocking bills in the latest Congress, and the latest is called the “Deterring Extraterritorial Foreign Exploitation of Networks Damaging Intellectual Property” aka the “   DEFEND IP Act   .” The problem is that instead of “defending IP,” this bill will incentivize censorship, overblocking, and bad faith attempts to block access to a website. DEFEND IP Act, and all of these site-blocking proposals, threaten the open web.     
  We keep seeing attempts to pass site-blocking legislation–from SOPA/PIPA in 2012 to    Block BEARD   ,    FADPA   , and    ACPA    this year. Every one of them has at its core the rotten idea that enforcing copyrights requires building a censorship machine for websites into the architecture of the internet. This is, of course, a disaster for a free and open web. There is no way to create a mechanism for blocking access to an entire website that does not invite both deliberate abuse and lots of collateral harm to free and lawful speech.

title: Congress Has Another Site-Blocking Bill, And This One Targets VPNs
body:
Congress is taking another run at site-blocking, a deeply flawed concept that would undermine basic internet infrastructure. Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA) has introduced the American Copyright Protection Act (ACPA),    H.R. 10364   , a bill that would give copyright owners a new legal tool to block Americans’ access to foreign websites accused of copyright infringement.   
  The basic idea is    all too     familiar   , and it’s still dangerous. A copyright owner first asks a court to label a foreign website a “foreign piracy site.” Once that happens, the copyright owner could seek orders requiring internet service providers, DNS providers, and—new and explicit in this bill—VPN providers to take “commercially reasonable steps” to stop their users in the United States from accessing those sites. The decision to label a website as a “foreign piracy site” can happen without the accused site even showing up in court to defend itself.   
  ACPA Goes Further Than Other Site-Blocking Proposals

 On October 1, 2026, Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York rejected the government’s motion to dismiss the lawsuit.  The case was filed in October 2025  on behalf of the United Automobile Workers (UAW), Communications Workers of America (CWA), and American Federation of Teachers (AFT). The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), Muslim Advocates (MA), and the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic (MFIA) represent the labor unions. 
 This decision is a victory: The Court held that claims that the government’s social media surveillance program is harming the unions’ members, as well as hampering the ability of the unions to associate with their members and potential members, can move forward.

title: Ola Bini Ordered to Leave Ecuador Under Obscure Accusations
body:
In a new blow to    Ola Bini’s    legal guarantees, Ecuadorean authorities retained the free software developer and security expert yesterday in Quito and ordered his immediate deportation from the country. He is barred from returning to Ecuador for 10 years.     
  According to    information released    by his lawyer, Bini was intercepted by a car with four people who identified themselves as immigration agents. He was then taken to an immigration office without further information or a formal order from a competent authority. There, officials told Bini that his visa had been revoked but didn’t show any supporting document.      
  Bini's defense    filed    a    habeas corpus    to safeguard his freedom and prevent his deportation. Yet, Ecuadorian authorities affirmed that the developer represents a threat or risk to public security and the state structure, and must leave the country. The ground for deportation is    a secret report    which allegedly asserts that Bini committed acts against the security of Ecuador. The defense could not access its contents.

title: We Demand More Information on How Marin Cops Illegally Shared Flock ALPR Data
body:
The Marin County Sheriff’s Office is the latest California law enforcement agency to get caught sharing automated license plate reader (ALPR) data from their Flock Safety system with out-of-state and federal agencies. EFF and the ACLU of Northern California are calling them out for this direct violation of California law, which has put every driver in the county at risk and is especially dangerous for immigrants, abortion seekers, and other targets of the federal government. 
 Today, we sent the Marin County Sheriff’s Office (MCSO) a demand letter and request for records under the California Public Records Act following the  Point Reyes Light’s recent report  that MCSO provided non-California agencies access to its ALPR database. This directly violates California law and the terms of the 2022  Settlement Agreement  in our case   Lagleva v. Marin County Sheriff  . 
  ALPRs  are cameras that capture images of vehicles and upload their location to a searchable, shareable database. They are a mass surveillance technology that collects data indiscriminately on every vehicle on the road.

title: Challengers Approach: Third Party App Stores Arrive to Google Play
body:
If you are an Android user, you may have noticed it already: Google has begun allowing rival, third-party app stores to be distributed through the Google Play Store. And if you are a developer, you may have noticed new options for billing and distributing your apps.   
  For    years,    Epic Games, maker of games such as Fortnite, has been suing Google, alleging violations of antitrust law. Specifically at issue were Google's restrictions on the distribution of alternate app stores through the Play Store, restrictions on app developers who have little practical choice but to distribute their apps through the Play Store, and Google’s rules governing in-app payments and the fees associated with them.   
  Epic’s challenge ultimately resulted in a court order requiring significant changes to Google’s practices. Among other changes, rival, third-party Android app stores are now allowed to access the Play Store’s catalog and to be distributed through the Google Play Store. Developers also have greater freedom to direct users to alternative payment and distribution options.

title: Court Agrees with EFF: Utah’s VPN Law Demands a Technical Impossibility
body:
When state lawmakers attempt to rewrite how the internet works, users rely on courts to recognize that laws can’t make technical impossibilities a reality. That’s why we were happy to see that a court has blocked Utah’s attempt to outlaw the privacy protections of Virtual Private Networks (VPNs).     
  In a win for digital rights, a federal judge has    issued a preliminary injunction    blocking Utah’s SB 73, the state’s draconian    anti-VPN age verification law   . The decision comes as EFF    submitted our comments    to the Utah Department of Commerce, detailing how forcing platforms to detect and block privacy-preserving tools undermines user privacy and security worldwide while demanding the impossible.      
   What SB 73 Does      
  Signed    into law earlier this year   , SB 73 attempted to regulate adult websites by requiring them to block VPN users or to identify the physical location of visitors using them or similar tools that mask their network traffic. It even went so far as to prohibit websites from offering instructions on how to use a VPN to bypass these checks. title: Happy Opt Out October! Let’s Find Real Alternatives to the Tech Giants
body:
Over the years, the major tech companies have found all sorts of ways to embed themselves into our lives. We often use their software, their AI tools, their social media, and their operating systems by default without even thinking about potential alternatives. It’s time to rethink that relationship.   
  Last year,    we created Opt Out October    to help remind ourselves of the variety of ways we can take back control of our data through small steps inside apps, operating systems, and other various forms. This year, we highlight the idea that sometimes the best way to control your data is to leave a platform, app, or operating system altogether.   
  To do so,    we’ve created a hub of resources sharing ways    to find new software that isn’t made by the tech giants, take advantage of the growing universe of new social media options, install a whole new operating system, and better control how various popular tools and software use your data for AI training.

CPDP (“Computers, Privacy and Data Protection”) is a non-profit platform founded in 2007 by research groups at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel, the Université de Namur, and Tilburg University, later joined by INRIA and the Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research. title: The Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) represents everything that’s wrong with Europe’s approach to digital sovereignty
body:
The EU’s Tech Sovereignty Package is supposed to jump-start Europe’s “sovereign AI” ambitions.  But due to fundamental misunderstandings about the technology behind ‘AI’ and the blind trust in Big Tech’s AI doomer and boomer narratives, it is more likely to instead hurt digital rights and the environment instead, and waste valuable public resources that should have been invested in actually increasing Europe’s digital resilience. The Cloud and AI Development (CADA) Act, a part of the Tech Sovereignty Package, adds up to an aggressive policy push to impose “European AI”. 
 The post  The Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) represents everything that’s wrong with Europe’s approach to digital sovereignty  appeared first on  European Digital Rights (EDRi) .

body:

EDRi member epicenter.works has sent an open letter to parliament, and is looking for input from readers elsewhere in Europe about how other countries are handling, or planning to handle, the same issue.

title: D3 brings class actions on addictive design against Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube
body:
The Portuguese digital rights organisation and EDRi member D3 announces that it has brought four class actions lawsuits against Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube over the use of addictive design practices. The cases challenge design practices that can encourage compulsive use of online platforms and seek to hold platforms accountable for the way their services affect users. Similar initiatives might come up in other EU Member States as part of a broader European response.

title: The KIDS Act will make the internet less safe
body:
On 16 September, the European Commission presented the KIDS ACT, its plan for making online experiences safer for young people. Far from being a move to lead the EU towards better digital environments, this move is a missed opportunity to address the root cause of why online platforms are harmful to children – and everyone else. This blog analyse the proposal’s shortcomings.

title: Serbia’s spyware scandal is also the EU’s problem
body:
At least 14 people in Serbia have been targeted with spyware since the beginning of 2026, according to new findings by EDRi member SHARE Foundation. The targets include members of the student movement, activists, a member of parliament from the opposition party and a local councillor. These findings comecame to light amid growing pressure on Serbia’s pro-democracy movement. The EU’s failure to address spyware at home undermines its credibility in demanding accountability from Serbia.

title: America's War Department Will Test Heat Ray Weapon For Potential Use
body:
Longtime Slashdot reader destinyland shares a report from CNN: The Pentagon has given the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a military-grade heat ray and develop tactics to potentially use it in operations at the southern US border, according to a memo signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month and obtained by CNN. The heat ray, officially known as the Active Denial System, is a nonlethal weapon that shoots an invisible beam of electromagnetic waves that can reach a little more than half a mile away, according to the US military. The energy beam causes a burning sensation when it comes into contact with the human skin -- which Pentagon officials have previously compared to feeling a blast of heat when opening a hot oven. Military officials have said the resulting "tingling effect" lasts between 10 and 15 minutes but also generates "an instinctive and irresistible urge to run from the effect."

Phages attack bacteria, and the hope is that this one will kill the microbes causing the infection.

They prompted Evo 2 to make new genomes similar to those in a group of phage species. The A.I. generated 700,000 virus genomes. The team synthesized DNA molecules from 285 genomes and inserted them into bacteria. The researchers found that 16 of the genomes gave rise to viable viruses. title: eBay to Cut 9% of Workforce
body:
eBay plans to cut about 1,000 jobs, or 9% of its workforce, as CEO Jamie Iannone moves to redirect resources toward the company's fastest-growing businesses. Reuters reports: The company had 12,300 employees at the end of last year. It also let go about 6% of its workforce, or 800 employees, in February as part of efforts to streamline operations. EBay has set itself apart from rivals by pushing into authenticated luxury goods, collectibles and refurbished products, which draw enthusiasts willing to pay more for valuable items. That has helped its shares rise nearly 40% this year, outperforming the benchmark S&P 500's around 12% gain.
 
"Our strategy is working," Iannone said in the memo, adding that "continuing to capture the significant opportunity ahead requires us to make thoughtful choices about where we focus and invest." He said affected staff would be informed in the coming days.  
   
   



    Read more of this story  at Slashdot.

title: AMD Brings Ryzen Overclocking Driver to Linux
body:
AMD has published Linux kernel patches for an official Ryzen overclocking driver that allows users to adjust CPU power and current limits through a firmware interface exposed via sysfs. Phoronix reports: AMD engineer Shyam Sundar S K posted the patches for the AMD Overclocking "AOD" WMI driver as an interface to the platform firmware for managing overclocking and power/current limits of modern Ryzen CPUs.
 
The driver in its initial form allows setting via sysfs a number of CPU tunables including the Package Power Tracking (PPT), Thermal Design Current (TDC), and Electrical Design Current (EDC) limits along with reading their supported range. SMT toggling can also be done via the interface as an alternative to the likes of Linux's "nosmt" option in disabling SMT at the platform level rather than kernel disabling. The current memory clocks can also be read via this AOD driver.
 
The power tunables aren't applied in real-time but go into effect at next reboot. The firmware does support many more commands compared to the few initially wired up and hopefully in time more of these controls will be enabled with this driver.  
   
   



    Read more of this story  at Slashdot.

title: More Than 1.5 Million Canadian Crime Stoppers Tips Leaked
body:
A CBC investigation found that more than 1.5 million Canadian Crime Stoppers tips spanning 25 years were exposed in a breach of the P3 Global Intel tip-management platform. About 850,000 records contained personally identifiable information, including addresses, phone numbers, emails, license plates and some banking details. Longtime Slashdot reader doconnor shares the report: The data was stolen last March by hacktivist collective Internet Yiff Machine. In a manifesto, the group said it wanted to disprove the claim by P3 Global Intel -- the company hired by Crime Stoppers to manage its tips -- that the platform was "anonymous" and "secure." A copy of the hacked data was made available to researchers and journalists, including CBC, by Distributed Denial of Secrets, a U.S. non-profit that archives and publishes hacked and leaked documents it deems to be in the public interest. The report found that more than 4,300 Crime Stoppers tipsters identified themselves by their full name, with hundreds of records containing staff warnings that individuals had "self-identified" or been "exposed," yet their information remained unredacted.

Quartz reports: Chief Studios Officer Cam Weber and Chief Operating Officer David Tinson wrote that "over the past several months, we've taken a hard look at our business." They said a small BioWare team had been doing early groundwork on a Mass Effect game, but EA chose to drop the effort. That decision means closing the studio and its Edmonton workspace, they wrote. "We do not take this decision lightly," Weber and Tinson said of the BioWare closure, according to Variety.
 
EA will keep investing in Apex Legends and is continuing work on two upcoming launches, Marvel's Iron Man and the next Star Wars Jedi game, the executives said. They added that EA's Respawn and DICE studios will join forces on an upcoming project, in addition to new Battlefield titles. title: Government Websites Go Dark After Severe PHP Vulnerabilities Disclosed

"As a result, government web sites in Europe and elsewhere temporarily went dark on Wednesday as operators worked to protect their systems." The Independent reports: Dane Knecht, the chief technology officer of Web and cloud security firm Cloudflare, said that attacks were emerging and Cloudflare was updating its firewall rules as a stopgap measure. title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security (PHP Foundation)
body:
The PHP Foundation has put out  a
blog entry  explaining how the vulnerabilities disclosed today came
about and why they took so long to fix.
 
 
	To fix the OOM problem, the PHP security team developed several
	competing approaches, but each came with its own trade-offs:
	backward compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service potential, or
	requiring changes to many third-party extensions which seemed
	impossible to coordinate. The PHP security team, operating on
	consensus, struggled to choose between these and feared the
	repercussions of shipping the wrong choice. Combined with the lack
	of a known path to remote code execution and the small team of core
	developers with the necessary deep knowledge of the engine occupied
	with many responsibilities, this decision process caused work on a
	fix to stall and restart repeatedly over months. We won't pretend
	otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the
	security team's decision process and its lack of resources.

title: Upstreaming Tyr: Rust, DRM, and the Linux Kernel (Collabora)
body:
The Collabora blog  provides
an update on Tyr , a driver for Arm Mali GPUs.
 
 
	One of our biggest challenges has been developing Tyr while the
	Rust kernel abstractions and driver interfaces are also being
	developed. As the driver interfaces are naturally revised and
	improved, we have rewritten Tyr several times to adapt to the
	larger Rust ecosystem. This not only makes progress much slower
	than it would be with a mature API, but also stalls progress for
	capabilities, such as job scheduling, while the abstraction is
	properly designed, reviewed, tested, and merged upstream.
 
	But working in this evolving environment is also precisely where
	Tyr is able to provide the most value. As a user of these new Rust
	abstractions, Tyr helps to expose their requirements and
	limitations.

title: [$] Understanding Nix flakes
body:
Nix flakes  are an
experimental feature of the  Nix package-management
tool  designed to build projects in a more self-contained and reproducible
way. Despite the feature's experimental status, it has become increasingly
popular for open-source projects to publish  flake.nix  files that offer
predefined development environments and build automation even when those
repositories may not offer an upstream package or module for the  NixOS Linux distribution . Although
Nix flakes have a complicated history, and the path for stabilization is
uncertain, flakes can provide useful capabilities for projects that choose to
include them.

title: PHP patches released for two critical RCEs
body:
The PHP project has  published  PHP
versions  8.5.12 ,
 8.4.27 ,  8.3.36  and  8.2.35  to address
two critical vulnerabilities that could allow unauthenticated remote code
execution. 

 
 Who is at risk:  all PHP installations serving web requests,
including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. We
consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an
unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code
runs. 

  The vulnerabilities:  

 
  RCE via OOM corruption , CVE-2026-109618 ( GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w ): out-of-memory
handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid. 
  RCE via stale global state , CVE-2026-109619 ( GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp ): request-owned
internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later
request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal
initialization resets it.

title: [$] SUSE's efforts to disable setuid system-wide
body:
Setuid (and setgid) binaries have long been a source of headaches, and security
vulnerabilities, on Linux systems. They are largely seen as something to be
avoided; SUSE's security team, for example,  forbids
the inclusion of setuid or setgid binaries in packages  unless they have been
reviewed and explicitly allowed. Thorsten Kukuk wants to go a step further and
disallow them entirely. At the  2026 All Systems Go!  conference, he spoke
about his work to disable setuid system-wide, as well as some of the hurdles
that remain.

title: [$] Discussing a rewrite of XArray
body:
The work to support block sizes larger than the page size on XFS has been
difficult. Many users of XFS run stable kernels, which means that they aren't testing
new XFS code as it is released. That has made Daniel Gomez wonder whether
adopting Rust for some of the data structures underlying XFS, particularly
 
XArrays , could reduce the number of bugs lurking in the code. At
Kangrejos 2026, he led a discussion about the potential problems with converting
XArray to Rust. The assembled kernel developers had a number of reasons to be
cautious about replacing the XArray code, but Gomez was determined to experiment
with the possibility, citing both security and performance improvements.

websites they do not control. An attacker who could intercept a user's
connection could use those certificates to impersonate websites and potentially
read or modify traffic.
 

 Mozilla has blocked the affected certificates using its  OneCRL 
centralized list of revoked certificates, and has updated the trusted
certificate list in  Network
Security Services (NSS) 3.131.1 . 

 There is a  single-page
site  about the compromise that goes into more detail. According to the site
the certificates have also been blocked in Chrome since October 17, Apple
devices since the 19th, and Microsoft blocked the certificates on the
20th. There is also a table that displays whether a browser or other client
still trusts the compromised certificates. 

 The NetBSD foundation has  issued
instructions  to block the certificates on NetBSD installations. Users of
other browsers and operating systems may wish to check for updates or guidance
to disable the compromised

title: Google ML Kit's barcode scanner adds the INTERNET permission and sends diagnostics, even in apps with no network code
body:
While checking one of my own apps with Exodus Privacy, I noticed it had the INTERNET permission even though the code never touches the network. The culprit turned out to be Google ML Kit's barcode scanning library, which a very popular Flutter QR scanner uses under the hood. It adds INTERNET and ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE through a Google transport library, and sends diagnostic data to Google when the scanner is opened (device model, app version, an install-scoped ID, latencies, error codes). Google documents this, but you'd never guess it from an app that just reads a QR code.

A few things I took away from it:
- A "0 trackers" result on Exodus doesn't mean "no network". Check the permission list too.
- If an app that should be offline asks for INTERNET, a QR/barcode feature is worth suspecting.
- For developers: ZXing-based scanners decode entirely on-device and don't pull any of this in. You can confirm with the merged manifest or the manifest-merger report in your build folder.

Has anyone else run into libraries quietly adding network access like this? Curious which others are common offenders.

title: Let's Encrypt to Cut SSL Certificate Lifetimes to 64 Days in February 2027
body:

>
>All certificates issued or renewed from that date will have a 64-day lifespan unless users explicitly select one of the shorter options already available: 45 or six days.
>
>Existing certificates will remain valid until their expiration dates. Let’s Encrypt expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The organization also confirmed no valid certificates will be revoked during the transition.
>
>To help administrators prepare, Let’s Encrypt will introduce 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026, allowing users to test their renewal setups before the change reaches production.
>
>The move is part of a broader effort to improve web security by reducing how long compromised or incorrectly issued certificates remain usable. Simply put, shorter certificate lifetimes mean attackers have less time to exploit a stolen private key.

Hi HN! We’re Srikar and Kevan, founders of Alter – https://alterauth.com/. We’re building access control for agents that can take actions on behalf of multiple users.

If you’ve built an internal agent people use through Slack, you may have experienced this scenario: everyone signs in with their own account, but the agent connects to the CRM or billing system with one shared API key, so the agent can do anything that the key can do. User-level authentication in Slack does nothing to control what the agent can do in an external system like the CRM or billing system.

Here’s what Alter does:

-It acts as a proxy and manages downstream credentials for every API request that an agent takes;

-It takes identity into account for every action the agent does. Automatically take into account the end user identity of the person that the agent is taking actions on behalf of.

title: Show HN: Jev Cards, Can you beat a vision model at a picture quiz?
body:
I built a quiz game around TypeSafe's new Jev model, which has vision capabilities. Jev looks at a picture and a question and picks an answer (or taps a place) in about a quarter of a second.

I've always loved quiz games and thought this would be a fun way to see what it can do and how fast it is. I made the cards from scratch, and Jev gets exactly the picture you see. More cards will come over time.

The code is open source, so feel free to build your own game or make more cards that I can publish.

Disclaimer: I ran Jev through both TypeSafe and Opper, and made the cards through Opper's vision models and Claude Code. I work at Opper, but jevcards is open source and free to play.

Maxwell sees programs from the inside: traces, profiling information, and the data flowing through them. It adapts dynamically to the environment, including the hardware, what else is running, and what the inputs look like.

title: Show HN: Check if any of the $656M in unclaimed royalties at The MLC is yours
body:
Hi HN, I built this. Quick background on why it exists:

When music is streamed on digital streaming platforms (think Spotify, Apple Music, Pandora), there are two separate royalty streams: one for the recording, paid through your distributor (DistroKid, TuneCore, CDBaby), and one for the underlying work (generally known as publishing). The work side's mechanical royalties are collected by The MLC, a nonprofit that was created by the 2018 Music Modernization Act (MMA). If you haven't registered your songs with The MLC, there are issues with your metadata, or about half a dozen other reasons, that money will never reach you, it just collects in a big pile we call the "black box".

That pile is big. The MLC's own dashboard currently shows over $656M is held (themlc.com/blanket-royalties), and the biggest problem is the MMA dictates that The MLC cannot hold that money indefinitely. At some point, by law, The MLC must distribute this big pile of cash, and since they don't know who it's supposed to go to, they pay it out through a process called "market share" (themlc.com/marketshare). - your first customer or pilot requires coverage before your machine can work on their site

title: Show HN: Let's Seal – Let's Encrypt for document signing, free and self-hosted
body:
TLDR, Let's Seal gives the finger to Adobe and every doc signing tool (docusign, google, etc) who pay to play with the Adobe Approved Trust List and then charge you for something that should be free.

Currently even the person checking if a document/contract is sealed or code is authentic has to also be inside the same Adobe walled garden too. Verification, the part that should be free is the part everyone charges for. Thats the shape Let's Encrypt fixed for TLS, and I wanted the same thing for documents and files.

The core idea therefore needed to go a bit beyond e signatures and i created an open standard (SEAL), plus free tools that implement it.

When you seal a file, three independent things happen.

1. it gets a signature from a certificate authority, chaining to a public root. 2. its record is appended to an RFC 6962 transparency log. and 3. its SHA256 is timestamped on a public blockchain (Bitcoin) via OpenTimestamps. Those three give you integrity, transparency and a timestamped proof. And importantly, none of those depend on Let's Seal and none are gated.

You can verify with the tools you already have, no Let's Seal account and no Let&#x

title: How to reliably retrieve all posts from a Facebook group going back to 2015 (search misses results, scrolling crashes around 2022)
body:
I'm a member of a Facebook group that has been posting content (trivia questions) since 2015, and I want to catalogue every post starting from the earliest one. 
 Problem 1 : Search is unreliable: Using Facebook's built-in search within the group doesn't return all posts from a given year. Some posts are omitted for no apparent reason, even when filtering by date. 
 Problem 2 : Scrolling crashes: Manually scrolling back through the group's history works up to a point, but once I reach posts from around 2022, the browser tab/app consistently crashes before I can get further back. 
 Constraint: The posts don't share consistent keywords or phrasing, so text-based search isn't a reliable filter. Filtering by month/year seems like the only practical approach, but I can't get it to work reliably.
What I'm looking for: 
 A reliable method or tool to filter/export Facebook group posts by date range
Any way to export or archive a group's full post history (browser extension, API, third-party tool, etc.) 
 A workaround for the crashing when scrolling through several years of content 
 Has anyone dealt with this before, and what worked for you?

title: 'Action Required' Sign in to Google Photos with your Google Account to keep your photos & videos
body:
I get these emails frequently with subject line "[Action Required] Sign in to Google Photos with your Google Account to keep your photos & videos". Every time it's from a different email. It seems to  be click bait and a security issue but there is no CVE related to it. 
 The email message contains 
 
 This is a copy of a security alert sent to <some_username@gmail.com>.
<myactualemail@gmail.com> is the recovery email for this account. If
you don't recognize this account, remove it. 
 
 But my email shouldn't be the recovery email of any of these accounts. 
 If anyone thinks all of a sudden, 50 different people are sharing photos with me, that's not normal. Does someone understand what this is? And why is Google not doing anything about this when their platform is being abused?
